title: FDA-Approved Drugs for Pediatric and Adolescent Obesity: Clinical Evidence and PREA Requirements
summary: FDA-approved pediatric obesity drugs, the pivotal adolescent trials and BMI endpoints behind them, and how PREA waivers, deferrals and Written Requests shaped each approval.
body_markdown:
## FDA-approved drugs for pediatric and adolescent obesity: clinical evidence and PREA requirements


FDA has approved five drugs whose current labeling establishes safety and effectiveness for weight management in pediatric patients. Four cover general (polygenic) obesity in adolescents aged 12 years and older: orlistat (Xenical), liraglutide (Saxenda), phentermine/topiramate extended-release (Qsymia) and semaglutide injection (Wegovy). The fifth, setmelanotide (Imcivree), is limited to rare genetic obesity (BBS or POMC, PCSK1 or LEPR deficiency, labeled from age 2) and acquired hypothalamic obesity (labeled from age 4). Each adolescent approval rested on one randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of roughly one year, with a BMI-based primary endpoint. The PREA history differs by product. For Saxenda, Qsymia and Wegovy, FDA waived the youngest age groups and deferred the older pediatric groups at adult approval. The later adolescent efficacy supplement then fulfilled the 12 to 17 year requirement. Xenical's adolescent data came from a pediatric Written Request linked to exclusivity. Imcivree was largely exempt from PREA because of orphan designation.

### Adolescent obesity approvals


#### Xenical (orlistat)


Xenical was the first of these products to gain adolescent labeling. FDA approved efficacy supplement S-018 on December 12, 2003. The supplement revised labeling for obesity management in adolescents aged 12 to 16[481](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=481)[477](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=477) . It responded to an FDA pediatric Written Request and sought a pediatric exclusivity determination[482](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=482) . The medical team leader memo states that Roche ran the two requested pediatric studies as the Written Request specified. A later clinical review describes the adolescent study as the basis for six months of exclusivity[483](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=483)[484](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=484) .


**Clinical evidence.** The pivotal study was a 54-week, multicenter, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 539 adolescents aged 12 to 16. Of these, 357 received orlistat 120 mg three times daily and 182 received placebo. Obesity was defined as a baseline BMI 2 units above the US weighted mean for the 95th percentile for age and sex[134](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=134)[135](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=135) . BMI was the primary efficacy parameter. After one year, mean BMI fell by 0.55 kg/m² with Xenical and rose by 0.31 kg/m² with placebo (p=0.001)[136](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=136) . Adolescent adverse effects were generally similar to those seen in adults, chiefly fatty or oily stool, oily spotting and oily evacuation. The label recommends a daily multivitamin containing fat-soluble vitamins[485](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=485) . The current label states that pediatric safety and effectiveness are established at 12 years and older[134](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=134) .


**Pediatric requirements.** The 1999 original approval letter deferred pediatric studies until December 2, 2000 and asked for a pediatric development plan[77](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=77) . Recent supplements (2015, 2016, 2022 and 2026) were exempt from PREA because none of the triggering criteria applied[73](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=73)[74](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=74)[75](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=75)[76](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=76) .


#### Saxenda (liraglutide 3 mg)


**PREA at adult approval.** The December 23, 2014 Saxenda approval letter waived pediatric studies for ages 0 to 6, inclusive, because the studies were impossible or highly impracticable. FDA explained that weight maintenance, not weight loss, is the goal for obese children aged 2 to 6. Weight loss is not recommended below age 2 because of growth and neurodevelopmental needs. FDA deferred studies for ages 7 to 17 because the product was ready for adult approval[276](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=276) . The PMR development templates describe PK/PD studies in patients aged 12 to 17 and 7 to 11[282](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=282)[283](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=283) .


**Fulfillment.** The December 4, 2020 supplement letter identifies PREA PMR 2802-03 as a 56-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study in patients aged 12 to 17. It states that S-012 contained the final report and that the requirement was fulfilled. Other PMRs from the 2014 letter remained open[277](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=277)[278](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=278)[279](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=279)[280](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=280)[281](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=281) .


**Clinical evidence.** The adolescent trial enrolled 251 pubertal patients aged 12 to 17 and began with a 12-week lifestyle run-in. Patients then received once-daily Saxenda or placebo for 56 weeks[560](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=560) . The primary endpoint was change in BMI standard deviation score (BMI SDS). At week 56, BMI SDS changed by −0.23 with Saxenda and −0.00 with placebo, an estimated treatment difference of −0.22 (95% CI −0.37 to −0.08; p=0.0022)[561](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=561) . Adverse reactions led 10.4% of Saxenda patients to discontinue, compared with none on placebo[562](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=562) . One Saxenda-treated pediatric patient (0.8%) developed pancreatitis[563](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=563) .


**Indication specifics.** Saxenda's pediatric indication requires body weight above 60 kg and an initial BMI corresponding to 30 kg/m² or greater for adults under international (Cole) cut-offs. It does not use a US percentile threshold[97](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=97)[98](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=98) . The current label states that safety and effectiveness have not been established below age 12[442](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=442)[443](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=443) .


#### Qsymia (phentermine and topiramate extended-release)


**PREA at adult approval.** The July 17, 2012 original approval letter waived studies for ages 0 to 6. FDA cited evidence that Qsymia would be ineffective and unsafe in this group, along with concerns about topiramate's pediatric safety and possible effects of both components on growth, development, learning, memory and behavior[219](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=219)[237](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=237) . Studies for ages 7 to 17 were deferred[238](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=238) . The PMR development templates set out four PREA studies[239](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=239)[243](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=243)[247](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=247)[251](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=251) :


Deferred PREA study Final protocol Study completion Final report

**Fulfillment.** The June 24, 2022 S-021 letter states that the pediatric study requirement for ages 12 to 17 has been fulfilled[255](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=255) .


**Clinical evidence.** Study 3 was a 56-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 223 patients aged 12 to 17 with BMI at or above the 95th percentile. Patients received placebo (n=56), Qsymia 7.5 mg/46 mg (n=54) or Qsymia 15 mg/92 mg (n=113), alongside lifestyle modification[302](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=302) . The primary efficacy parameter was mean percent change in BMI at week 56[535](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=535) .

Thirty-eight percent of randomized patients withdrew before week 56. Missing data were imputed with a placebo-based washout method[540](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=540)[541](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=541) .


**Pediatric safety.** Height velocity was 1.3 to 1.4 cm/year lower with Qsymia than with placebo[583](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=583) . Mood-related reactions and sleep disorders were more frequent with Qsymia. Depression occurred in 0%, 2% and 4% of the placebo, low-dose and high-dose groups[584](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=584)[585](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=585) . A heart rate increase of more than 10 bpm at a single time point occurred in 46.4%, 55.6% and 64.6% of the respective groups[592](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=592) .


#### Wegovy (semaglutide 2.4 mg injection)


**PREA at adult approval.** The June 4, 2021 original approval letter waived pediatric studies under age 6. FDA found no meaningful therapeutic benefit over existing therapies and did not expect use in a substantial number of these patients[319](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=319)[325](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=325) . The review records an agreed deferral for ages 6 to under 18[326](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=326) .


**Fulfillment and indication.** FDA approved efficacy supplement S-005 on December 23, 2022. The letter states that the pediatric study requirement for ages 12 to under 18 was fulfilled. A PREA PMR from the 2021 letter remained open[308](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=308)[327](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=327) . The resulting indication covered pediatric patients aged 12 years and older with an initial BMI at or above the 95th percentile for age and sex[202](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=202)[203](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=203) . The November 27, 2024 S-015 supplement added 1.7 mg once weekly as an additional maintenance dose for patients aged 12 to under 18[461](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=461) . That letter marked PMR 4472-1, exposure and exposure-response analyses supporting the 1.7 mg pediatric dose, as fulfilled[463](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=463) . It also restated that the 12 to 17 requirement was fulfilled[331](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=331) .


**Clinical evidence.** The pediatric trial (Study 7, NCT04102189) was a 68-week, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled, multicenter trial[462](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=462) . It enrolled 201 pubertal patients aged 12 and older with BMI at or above the 95th percentile. After a 12-week lifestyle run-in, patients were randomized 2:1. A 16-week escalation to 2.4 mg (or the maximum tolerated dose) was followed by 52 weeks of maintenance. The primary endpoint was percent change in BMI to week 68[395](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=395)[396](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=396) .

**Pediatric safety.** Compared with Wegovy-treated adults, pediatric patients had higher incidences of cholelithiasis, cholecystitis, hypotension, rash and urticaria[624](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=624) . Cholelithiasis occurred in 3.8% of pediatric Wegovy patients and 0% of pediatric placebo patients, versus 1.6% of Wegovy-treated adults[625](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=625)[626](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=626) . Nausea (42% vs 18%) and vomiting (36% vs 10%) were the most common pediatric adverse reactions[627](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=627) .


**Ongoing PREA obligations.** A July 21, 2023 supplement letter again waived pediatric studies under age 6 and deferred studies for ages 6 to 18[328](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=328) . For the MASH indication (S-024, August 15, 2025), FDA waived studies under age 6 and deferred studies for ages 6 to under 17. PMR 4882-2 requires a randomized, placebo-controlled trial in patients aged 6 to under 17 with non-cirrhotic MASLD with fibrosis, with a final report due January 2030[332](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=332)[333](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=333)[334](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=334)[335](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=335) . The oral Wegovy tablet (NDA 218316, approved December 22, 2025) has no pediatric indication[209](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=209)[151](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=151) . Its review anticipates a PREA PMR for population PK and exposure-response analyses in patients aged 12 to under 18[214](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=214) .


### Rare genetic and hypothalamic obesity: Imcivree (setmelanotide)


Imcivree is indicated to reduce excess body weight and maintain weight reduction in adults and pediatric patients with specific causes of obesity. These are acquired hypothalamic obesity (age 4 and older) and Bardet-Biedl syndrome (BBS) or POMC, PCSK1 or LEPR deficiency (age 2 and older). It is not indicated for general (polygenic) obesity[177](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=177) .


**Approval sequence.**


- November 25, 2020: original approval for POMC/PCSK1 and LEPR deficiency in patients aged 6 and older. After one year, 8 of 10 POMC/PCSK1 patients (80%) and 5 of 11 LEPR patients (45.5%) achieved at least 10% weight loss. These results pool adults and children; 38% of the efficacy population was aged 16 or younger[414](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=414)[415](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=415)[416](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=416) .
- June 16, 2022: BBS added for patients aged 6 and older, based on a 66-week study with a 14-week randomized, placebo-controlled period followed by 52 weeks of open-label treatment. The study included 22 participants aged 6 to 17[417](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=417)[418](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=418)[419](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=419) .
- December 20, 2024: extension to ages 2 to under 6, based on a 52-week open-label trial in 12 children (3 POMC, 4 LEPR, 5 BBS)[422](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=422)[423](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=423) .
- March 19, 2026: acquired hypothalamic obesity added for patients aged 4 and older[424](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=424)[425](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=425) . Trial 1 randomized 142 patients aged 4 and older (94 Imcivree, 48 placebo); 31% were aged 12 to under 18 and 23% were aged 4 to under 12[179](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=179)[180](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=180)[181](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=181) . At week 52, BMI fell by 15.84% with Imcivree and rose by 2.55% with placebo. The placebo-adjusted difference was −18.40 points (95% CI −21.94 to −14.85), in the combined adult and pediatric population[182](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=182)[183](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=183) .


**PREA status.** The original application was exempt from PREA because setmelanotide held orphan designation for POMC (including PCSK1) and LEPR deficiency[108](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=108) . The 2022 BBS supplement was likewise exempt on orphan grounds[109](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=109) . The December 2024 supplement was exempt because no PREA trigger applied[110](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=110) . For the 2026 hypothalamic obesity supplement, FDA waived studies from birth to under 4 years as impossible or highly impracticable[111](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=111) .


### Products without a pediatric obesity indication


**Zepbound (tirzepatide).** Current labeling states that safety and effectiveness have not been established in pediatric patients[504](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=504)[507](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=507) . At the November 8, 2023 weight-management approval, FDA waived studies for ages 0 to 5. It found no meaningful therapeutic benefit and did not expect substantial use in that group[363](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=363)[367](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=367) . FDA agreed to defer studies for ages 6 to under 18[366](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=366) . The deferred program includes a 72-week safety and efficacy trial in adolescents aged 12 to 17, with study completion due February 2027 and a final report due August 2027[368](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=368)[369](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=369)[370](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=370) . It also includes a PK/PD dose-selection study in children aged 6 to 11[371](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=371)[372](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=372) . The obstructive sleep apnea supplement (December 20, 2024) added PMR 4759-1, a 72-week study in adolescents with obesity-related OSA, with a draft protocol due June 2031[374](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=374)[375](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=375)[376](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=376) .


**Adipex-P (phentermine).** The label states that pediatric safety and effectiveness have not been established. It does not recommend use for pediatric obesity, which requires long-term treatment, because Adipex-P is approved only for short-term therapy[344](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=344) . The label also states that Adipex-P is not recommended for patients aged 16 or younger[345](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=345) .


### The PREA pattern and current FDA expectations


Saxenda, Qsymia and Wegovy show a consistent template. At adult approval, FDA waived the youngest children, citing ages 0 to 6 or under 6. The waiver rationale was either that weight loss is not the treatment goal in that group or that the product offers no meaningful benefit there[276](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=276)[237](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=237)[325](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=325) . FDA deferred older pediatric groups to postmarketing requirements[276](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=276)[238](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=238)[326](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=326) . A later adolescent efficacy supplement then fulfilled the 12 to 17 requirement[277](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=277)[255](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=255)[327](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=327) . The requirements for the 6 or 7 to 11 year cohort remain the open part of these programs. None of the current labels for these products establishes use below age 12[442](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=442)[134](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=134) .


FDA's January 7, 2025 draft guidance, *Obesity and Overweight: Developing Drugs and Biological Products for Weight Reduction* , sets out these expectations[606](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=606) :


- Include children aged 6 and older, generally in separate trials or cohorts for adolescents (12 and older) and children (6 to 11)[607](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=607) .
- Generally enroll patients with BMI at or above the 95th percentile, or at or above the 85th percentile with a weight-related comorbidity in adolescents, after documented insufficient response to lifestyle modification[608](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=608) .
- Use a BMI-based primary endpoint, such as mean percent change in BMI, because children are still growing[609](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=609) .
- Run randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials of at least one year at the target dose[610](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=610) .
- Submit the initial pediatric study plan no later than 60 days after the end-of-phase 2 meeting. Adult efficacy and safety data should generally be available before pediatric studies of a new drug begin[611](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=611) .
- Meet PREA obligations with age-appropriate formulations unless a waiver, deferral or exception applies[612](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=612) .


The adolescent trials behind the approved products used different primary endpoints: absolute BMI change for Xenical, BMI SDS for Saxenda, and percent BMI change for Qsymia and Wegovy[136](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=136)[561](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=561)[535](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=535)[396](https://rhizomeai.com/articles/fda-approved-drugs-for-pediatric-and-adolescent?showSourceNumber=396) . Because of this variation, labeled effect sizes cannot be compared directly across products. The draft guidance's preference for percent change in BMI is likely to make future pediatric programs more comparable.
